(CNN) -- A New York Times reporter who was held by the Taliban for seven months has escaped, the newspaper reported Saturday. New York Times reporter David Rohde, shown in 1995, escaped from the Taliban. David Rohde told his wife, Kristen Mulvihill, that he and a local reporter, Tahir Ludin, climbed over the wall of a compound late Friday where they were being held in the North Waziristan region of Pakistan. Pakistani military spokesman Gen. Athar Abbas told CNN that the Pakistani military was involved in freeing Rohde. Additional details were not immediately available. U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton issued a statement expressing her relief about Rohde's "return to freedom." "I would like to thank the governments of Pakistan and Afghanistan for their assistance in ensuring his safe return," Clinton said. "Journalists put themselves at risk every day to report the news in regions gripped by conflict. We rely on their vital role and I am grateful for their service."  Watch CNN's Nic Robertson report on the escape » . Rohde, Ludin and their driver were kidnapped outside of Kabul, Afghanistan, on November 10, and Afghan and Western officials said recently that Rohde was being held in Pakistan. After leaving the compound Friday night, the two men then found a Pakistani army scout who led them to a nearby army base. On Saturday, they were flown to Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan, the newspaper said. A U.S. official told CNN that Rohde will arrive in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates at 10 p.m. Saturday. "They just walked over the wall of the compound," Mulvihill said, according to the newspaper. Ludin hurt his foot during the escape, but otherwise both men appear to be in good health, the newspaper said. The driver, Asadullah Mangal, did not escape, the newspaper said. "It is hard to describe the enormous relief we felt at hearing the news of David and Tahir's escape and knowing he is safe," a statement from Rohde's family said. "Every day during these past seven months, we have hoped and prayed for this moment," said the statement, which was provided to CNN by The New York Times . It asked that the family's privacy be respected. White House press secretary Robert Gibbs said the White House was "very pleased to see that David Rohde is now safe and returning home." "This marks the end of a long and difficult ordeal for David's family, friends and co-workers. The FBI has been the lead agency on his case, and we refer you to them for any further information," he said. The New York Times and other media outlets had kept the kidnapping quiet out of concern for the men's safety. "From the early days of this ordeal, the prevailing view among David's family, experts in kidnapping cases, officials of several governments and others we consulted, was that going public could increase the danger to hostages," The New York Times said in a written statement. "Therefore, we did not publicly discuss the kidnapping. We are deeply grateful to the other news organizations that honored our request to refrain from reporting on it." A Taliban spokesman told CNN several weeks ago that the Taliban had released two "proof of identity" videos and had demanded negotiations. The Taliban wanted some of its leaders in U.S. custody to be released as well as money, the spokesman said. Rohde, 41, had traveled to Kabul in early November to work on a book, The New York Times said. He won a Pulitzer Prize in 1996 for his reporting on the Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia while working for The Christian Science Monitor. He was also part of The New York Times reporting team that won a Pulitzer Prize in May for coverage of Afghanistan and Pakistan last year.

The Times said Rohde and Ludin escaped late Friday by climbing over a wall at a compound where they were being held in Pakistan’s tribal areas. The two men then made their way to a Pakistani military checkpoint.

Mangal’s status was not immediately clear at the time of the announcement.

The kidnapping had been kept largely out of the public eye at the request of Rohde’s family and the Times, which said it feared publicity could increase the danger to the captives.

“We are enormously relieved,” Times executive editor Bill Keller said in a statement, praising those who worked behind the scenes to secure Rohde’s release.

Rohde, who has reported extensively from conflict zones, won a Pulitzer Prize in the 1990s for coverage of the Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia. He later covered Afghanistan, Pakistan and other international security issues.

His abduction underscored the risks facing journalists in the region, where militants and criminal networks have targeted reporters, aid workers and officials for ransom or political leverage.

The Taliban and affiliated militant groups have long operated across the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, particularly in Pakistan’s tribal areas, where foreign captives have sometimes been moved to evade detection.

**David Rohde and Tahir Ludin Escape Taliban Captivity in Pakistan**

**NEW YORK / WASHINGTON —** David Rohde, a Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter for *The New York Times*, and Tahir Ludin, an Afghan journalist working with him, escaped from a Taliban compound in Pakistan after more than seven months in captivity, U.S. officials and *The New York Times* said.

Rohde and Ludin fled late Friday from a militant-held compound in Pakistan’s tribal areas, near the Afghan border, after being kidnapped in November 2008 while reporting outside Kabul. The two men reportedly climbed over a wall and made their way to safety, eventually reaching Pakistani security forces.

Their escape ended a long and closely guarded ordeal that had been kept largely out of the public eye at the request of *The New York Times* and Rohde’s family. Many news organizations agreed not to report the abduction, fearing publicity could increase the danger to the hostages.

Rohde, Ludin, and their driver, Asadullah Mangal, were seized on Nov. 10, 2008, while traveling to interview a Taliban commander in Logar Province, south of Kabul. They were later moved across the border into Pakistan’s tribal region, where militant groups maintained strongholds.

Mangal was not with Rohde and Ludin when they escaped.

### Clinton: “Very pleased” by the escape

Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton welcomed the news, saying U.S. officials were relieved that Rohde and Ludin had reached safety.

Clinton said she was “very pleased” to learn of their escape and praised efforts by those who had worked to secure their release. She also noted the dangers faced by journalists working in conflict zones, especially in Afghanistan and Pakistan, where reporters have often been targeted by insurgent groups.

### White House welcomes their safe return

The White House also issued a statement welcoming the escape and expressing relief that Rohde and Ludin were safe. Officials said the case underscored both the risks of reporting in war zones and the continuing threat posed by extremist networks operating along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.

The Obama administration had been closely monitoring the situation, though officials released few details about any diplomatic or security efforts while the men were captive.

### New York Times expresses relief

At *The New York Times*, executives said they were deeply relieved by the escape.

Bill Keller, then the newspaper’s executive editor, said the paper was overjoyed that Rohde and Ludin were free. Times officials also thanked other news organizations for honoring the request to withhold coverage of the kidnapping during the captivity.

The newspaper said the blackout was intended to avoid raising the hostages’ value to their captors or provoking additional threats against them. Such voluntary media silence is unusual but has occurred in some kidnapping cases involving journalists.

Arthur Sulzberger Jr., the publisher of *The New York Times*, also expressed gratitude to those who helped during the crisis and to Rohde’s family for their endurance throughout the months-long ordeal.

### A dangerous assignment

Rohde, a veteran foreign correspondent, had reported extensively on Afghanistan, Pakistan, and the Balkans. He shared a Pulitzer Prize in 1996 for reporting on the Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia and was part of a *New York Times* team that won a Pulitzer for coverage of Afghanistan and Pakistan.

At the time of his kidnapping, Rohde was working on a book about the region and had sought an interview with a Taliban figure. Ludin, an experienced Afghan journalist, was assisting him.

Their abduction highlighted the growing dangers faced by journalists in Afghanistan and Pakistan as insurgent violence intensified. Militants in the border region had increasingly used kidnappings for ransom, propaganda, and leverage against foreign governments.

Rohde and Ludin’s escape brought an end to one of the most closely held kidnapping cases involving a major American journalist during the Afghan war.

**Kidnapped New York Times Reporter David Rohde and Afghan Colleague Escape Taliban Captivity**

**NEW YORK/KABUL —** New York Times reporter **David Rohde** and Afghan journalist **Tahir Ludin** have escaped after more than seven months in captivity, ending a prolonged ordeal that began when the two men were kidnapped by militants while working on a reporting assignment outside Kabul.

The Times said Rohde and Ludin fled their captors late Friday, escaping from a compound in the Taliban-influenced tribal region along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. The two men had been held since **Nov. 10, 2008**, when they were abducted while traveling to interview a Taliban commander.

Rohde, a Pulitzer Prize-winning correspondent, and Ludin, an Afghan reporter and interpreter who was assisting him, were seized along with their driver, **Asadullah Mangal**, after leaving Kabul for a meeting connected to Rohde’s reporting on the war in Afghanistan. Their abduction occurred in an area near the capital where Taliban-linked militants had grown increasingly bold despite the heavy presence of Afghan and international forces.

According to accounts released after the escape, Rohde and Ludin had been moved between locations in Afghanistan and Pakistan during their captivity. They eventually escaped by slipping away from their guards and making contact with Pakistani security forces. Both men were reported to be in good condition after reaching safety.

Mangal, their Afghan driver, was not part of the escape, and his status remained a major concern.

The kidnapping had been kept largely out of public view for months. The New York Times, joined by other news organizations, maintained a rare media blackout at the request of Rohde’s family and in consultation with officials, out of concern that publicity could increase the danger to the hostages or raise the kidnappers’ ransom demands.

Rohde, then a veteran foreign correspondent for the Times, had reported extensively from conflict zones including Afghanistan, Pakistan and the Balkans. He won a Pulitzer Prize as part of the team that covered Afghanistan and Pakistan after the Sept. 11 attacks, and earlier shared in a Pulitzer for his reporting on the Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia.

His kidnapping underscored the escalating risks faced by journalists, Afghan fixers, interpreters and drivers covering the Afghan war. By late 2008, insurgent groups had expanded their reach beyond traditional strongholds in southern and eastern Afghanistan, carrying out abductions, roadside bombings and attacks even near Kabul.

The circumstances of the abduction reflected one of the most dangerous dilemmas of war reporting: the need to interview insurgents and power brokers in order to understand the conflict, while traveling through areas where shifting alliances and criminal networks can quickly turn a reporting trip into a hostage crisis.

Rohde had been working on a book project related to Afghanistan when the kidnapping occurred. Ludin, an experienced Afghan journalist, had helped arrange contacts and navigate the local environment, roles that often place Afghan media workers at equal or greater risk than the foreign correspondents they assist.

The escape brought relief to colleagues and family members who had spent months working quietly behind the scenes to secure the men’s release. But it also left unresolved questions about the network that held them, the conditions of their captivity and the fate of Mangal.

For the Times and the broader journalism community, the episode marked both a rare piece of good news in a brutal conflict and a stark reminder of the dangers borne by reporters and local colleagues trying to cover wars from the ground.

**Freed U.S. journalist David Rohde returns after Taliban kidnapping; media silence aimed to protect captives**

*By [Reporter Name], CNN*  
*June 2009*

American journalist David Rohde has returned to freedom after more than seven months in captivity, ending a kidnapping ordeal that was kept largely out of public view by major news organizations at the request of his family and employer.

Rohde, a reporter for *The New York Times*, escaped from Taliban captivity in Pakistan along with Afghan journalist Tahir Ludin, the newspaper said. The two men had been held since November, when they were abducted while reporting in Afghanistan. Their driver, Asadullah Mangal, was also kidnapped and was later reported to have escaped separately.

The abduction began when Rohde and his colleagues were traveling to interview a Taliban commander, according to accounts released after his escape. They were taken by militants and eventually moved across the border into Pakistan’s tribal areas, a region that has long served as a sanctuary for Taliban and al Qaeda-linked fighters.

Rohde’s family said it was “filled with joy and relief” at his return, while also asking for privacy as he recovered from the ordeal.

“We are enormously relieved,” *New York Times* Executive Editor Bill Keller said in a statement after Rohde’s escape. Keller said the newspaper had worked closely with Rohde’s family and U.S. officials while he was missing.

A rare media blackout

One of the most unusual aspects of the case was the near-total silence surrounding it.

For months, dozens of news organizations — including television networks, newspapers and wire services — knew Rohde had been kidnapped but agreed not to report it. The decision was made because Rohde’s family and *The New York Times* believed publicity could increase his value to the kidnappers and put his life in greater danger.

Keller said the paper concluded early on that “publicity would raise David’s value to his captors and reduce his chance of survival.” Other media outlets honored the request, despite the case involving a well-known American journalist.

Such decisions are rare and controversial. News organizations generally resist withholding information, especially in matters involving public safety, war or terrorism. But in kidnapping cases, editors sometimes agree to keep details quiet if law enforcement, families or employers believe coverage could complicate negotiations or provoke captors.

In Rohde’s case, the concern was that public attention could transform the kidnapping into a higher-profile political act, prompting demands for ransom, prisoner releases or propaganda concessions.

A veteran correspondent

Rohde is a veteran foreign correspondent who has reported extensively from conflict zones. He won a Pulitzer Prize as part of a team covering Bosnia in the 1990s and later reported on Afghanistan, Pakistan and the broader U.S. fight against terrorism.

He was kidnapped at a particularly volatile moment in the Afghan war. Taliban influence had expanded in parts of Afghanistan and Pakistan, and militants were increasingly targeting government officials, aid workers, journalists and foreign contractors.

Rohde’s escape came after months of uncertainty and private diplomatic efforts. Details of how he and Ludin got away were initially limited, but *The New York Times* reported that the men escaped from a militant compound and made their way to Pakistani security forces.

The newspaper said no ransom was paid.

Press freedom risks

Rohde’s kidnapping underscored the dangers facing journalists in Afghanistan and Pakistan, where reporters often work between insurgent groups, criminal networks, local power brokers and government forces.

Media freedom groups have long warned that local journalists face the greatest risks, often with less protection and less international attention than Western correspondents. Ludin, the Afghan journalist kidnapped alongside Rohde, shared the same dangers throughout the captivity.

Rohde’s return brought relief to his family, colleagues and the wider journalism community — and renewed debate over how news organizations should handle kidnappings of reporters.

For months, the story was deliberately kept out of headlines. Only after Rohde was safe did the public learn how many people had known — and why they chose not to publish.

As Keller put it, the silence was intended for one purpose: to help bring Rohde home alive.
